authorship: Original practice written for this portal; class worksheets are not reproduced.
editorialReview: Every prompt gives a specific communicative intention, number, destination, direction or preference. Distractors contradict that detail or answer a different question.
Every correct response uses present-tense language, an infinitive after a modal, or a short fixed phrase. There is no requirement to conjugate past, future, conditional or subjunctive forms.
Service encounters consistently address staff or strangers politely; classmate and friend conversations use informal tu.
Grammar notes distinguish origin from current location, clock times from prices, singular piace from plural nouns, age with avere, and the reflexive pronoun in mi sveglio.
Scene introductions gloss less familiar task words. Hints support meaning or form; explanations disclose the answer and contrast its distractors.
All identities, plans and routines are fictional; no personal information is needed to practise.
Each of the 24 turns has a specific grammar unit link. Age opens avere, daily work opens present -are, and food preferences open piacere. Scene-level links remain available for broader study.
limitations: This is a model editorial review, not an independent native-speaker assessment or externally validated CEFR rating.
Multiple-choice recognition cannot certify spontaneous speaking, pronunciation, listening comprehension or A2 readiness.
A few practical phrases such as da quale binario and basta così are scaffolded chunks; beginners may need the English introduction and hint.
A learner who already knows numbers may find quantity and clock-time distractors easy; pair this content with supported spoken recall or sentence production in the UI.
